Your wet washcloth, wrung out in space, grows a skin of water that clings around the cloth and hand instead of dripping. Chris Hadfield showed this on camera aboard the ISS.
Your squeezed water blob in space floats as a perfect wobbling sphere. An effervescent tablet dropped in makes bubbles that stay trapped inside the ball.
Your sleep in space happens in a bag strapped to the wall, and your arms float up in front of you. Astronauts have to tether themselves down to sleep.
Your face puffs up in space because body fluids shift toward the head, while the legs get thinner. Astronaut photos show the puffy face.
Your daily workout on the ISS is about 2 hours strapped to a treadmill with a harness, or lifting on a vacuum-piston machine. Without it, bones and muscles waste away.
Your toilet in space works by suction, with thigh bars or straps to hold you down. The air flow pulls waste away because nothing falls on its own.
Your sandwich in space is a tortilla. Bread makes crumbs that float into equipment and eyes, so ISS crews eat tortillas instead.
Your zinnia flowers bloomed on the ISS in 2016, grown in space in a plant chamber. Astronaut Scott Kelly shared the photos, and the orange flower is real.
Your helmet filled with water during Luca Parmitano's 2013 spacewalk. Water pooled around his head and covered his eyes and nose, and he had to rush back inside.
Your 8-day trip turned into about 286 days for Sunita Williams. She launched on Starliner in June 2024 and only came back to Earth in March 2025.
Your Indian flag went to the ISS with Shubhanshu Shukla, the first Indian on the station, on the Axiom-4 mission launched in June 2025.
Your 1984 space trip had Rakesh Sharma answering Indira Gandhi's question about how India looks from space with 'Saare Jahan Se Accha'. He was the first Indian in space.
Your 2 rupee note once carried a satellite. India's first satellite, Aryabhata, launched in 1975 and appeared on the back of the 2 rupee note.
Your idea of a rocket launch breaks at ISRO's early days, when rocket parts were carried to the launch site on a bicycle. A famous photo also shows a satellite moved on a bullock cart.
Your single rocket launch carried 104 satellites on ISRO's PSLV-C37 in February 2017. It was a world record at the time.
Your Moon landing map has India at the south pole. Chandrayaan-3 touched down near the lunar south pole on 23 August 2023 and rolled out the Pragyan rover.
Your first-attempt Mars mission was India's. Mangalyaan reached Mars orbit in September 2014 on ISRO's first try, making India the first Asian country to do it.
Your Hindi, Tamil, Telugu and Bengali greetings are on a gold record flying through space. The Voyager Golden Record carries greetings in 55 languages and Indian classical music by Kesarbai Kerkar.
Your whole world, photographed by Voyager 1 from about 6 billion km away, is less than one pixel. It is the Pale Blue Dot photo, taken in 1990.
Your message from Voyager 1, launched in 1977, now takes close to a full day to reach Earth. The probe is still sending data from interstellar space.
Your car is in space. In February 2018 SpaceX launched a red Tesla Roadster with a mannequin called Starman, and it is still orbiting the Sun.
Your footprints on the Moon will not blow away. With no wind or water, the Apollo boot prints can stay for millions of years.
Your flag on the Moon did not survive the Apollo 11 departure. Buzz Aldrin said the lander's exhaust knocked it over as they lifted off.
Your hammer and feather fell together on the Moon. Apollo 15 astronaut David Scott dropped both at once on camera in 1971 and they landed at the same time.
Your golf game on the Moon happened. Alan Shepard hit golf balls on Apollo 14 in 1971 with a club head he attached to a tool handle.
Your car is still parked on the Moon. Three Apollo lunar rovers, from Apollo 15, 16 and 17, were left behind where the crews drove them.
Your white spacesuit turned black on the Moon. Apollo 17's Gene Cernan came back covered in sticky lunar dust, which clung to the suits and tools.
Your trash is on the Moon too. Apollo crews left behind about 96 bags of human waste, along with boots, tools and cameras.
Your tree might have been to the Moon. Seeds that orbited the Moon on Apollo 14 were planted on Earth as 'Moon trees'.
Your Apollo 13 rescue ran on duct tape. Engineers fitted a square carbon-dioxide filter to a round hole using socks, tape and cardboard, and the crew survived.
Your rocket launch can get hit by lightning. Apollo 12 was struck twice in the first minute after liftoff in 1969, then flew on to the Moon.
Your trash fine from Australia is real. After Skylab fell on Western Australia in 1979, the town of Esperance fined NASA 400 dollars for littering, and it was paid in 2009.
Your total solar eclipse is possible because the Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and about 400 times farther away. The Moon covers the Sun almost exactly.
Your Moon is moving away from Earth by about 3.8 cm a year, measured by mirrors left by Apollo astronauts.
Your bathtub could float Saturn. Saturn is less dense than water, so a giant enough ocean would let the planet float.
Your view of Saturn's north pole shows a six-sided hexagon cloud pattern. Cassini photographed this jet stream, a hexagon wider than Earth.
Your Uranus rolls like a ball around the Sun, tilted on its side by about 98 degrees. Its rings and moons circle it vertically.
Your Mars sunset is blue. Rover images show the sky around the setting Sun turning blue because of the fine dust in the air.
Your Mount Everest would look small next to Olympus Mons on Mars. The volcano is about 22 km high, roughly two and a half times Everest's height above sea level.
Your moon Phobos at Mars rises in the west and sets in the east, because it orbits faster than Mars spins. It is slowly spiralling inward.
Your helicopter flew on another planet. NASA's Ingenuity made the first powered flight on Mars in April 2021 and then flew 72 times.
Your robot built for 90 days lasted about 15 years. NASA's Opportunity rover roamed Mars from 2004 to 2018 and was often cleaned by wind gusts.
Your camera on Venus survived the 465 degree heat for about two hours. The Soviet Venera 13 sent back the first colour photos of Venus's surface in 1982.
Your landing on Titan in 2005 showed rounded pebbles and a riverbed. The Huygens probe photographed the surface of Saturn's moon, which has methane lakes.
Your water geysers on Saturn's moon Enceladus spray ice into space from cracks at its south pole. Cassini flew through the plumes and photographed them.
Your Jupiter moon Ganymede is bigger than the planet Mercury. It is the largest moon in the Solar System.
Your photo of Pluto shows a giant heart. New Horizons in 2015 found Tombaugh Regio, a heart-shaped plain of nitrogen ice.
Your comet looks like a rubber duck. Rosetta orbited comet 67P in 2014, and its two-lobed shape is easy to see in the photos.
Your asteroid was hit on purpose and moved. In 2022 NASA's DART crashed into Dimorphos and shortened its orbit around Didymos by about 32 minutes.
Your fastest human-made object is the Parker Solar Probe, which touched the Sun's corona and reached about 692,000 km/h in December 2024.
Your hair wash in space has no running water. Astronaut Karen Nyberg showed on camera how rinseless shampoo clings to her hair and her long hair floats up like a cloud.
Your toothpaste in space gets swallowed or wiped into a towel, because there is no sink and spit would float. Astronauts brush with a floating blob of paste on camera.
Your haircut in space uses clippers attached to a vacuum hose, so the cut hair is sucked straight in instead of floating around the cabin.
Your coffee cup in space has a sharp inner corner, and the coffee crawls up it by itself. This is the ISS zero-gravity cup from 2015, where surface tension does the work.
Your wing nut spun in space flips over and over by itself. The Dzhanibekov effect makes a spinning T-handle tumble in zero gravity, and it is visible on camera.
Your eyes see flashes of light with your eyelids closed in space. Astronauts have reported these streaks and sparks, which are linked to cosmic rays hitting the eye.
Your tacos were grown in space. In 2021 astronauts harvested Hatch chile peppers on the ISS and ate them in tacos, shown in the photos.
Your window on the ISS looks down on the aurora. Astronauts fly straight over glowing green curtains of light, and the photos show the green ripple from above.
Your rocket booster lands upright on its own legs. In December 2015, SpaceX's Falcon 9 first stage touched down standing on a pad, the first orbital rocket to do it.
Your space shuttle used to fly piggyback. NASA carried the orbiter on top of a modified Boeing 747 across the US, and photos show a jumbo jet carrying a spaceship.
Your rocket booster was caught by giant mechanical arms. In October 2024, SpaceX's Starship Super Heavy returned to its tower and was caught mid-air by the 'chopsticks'.
Your Pragyan rover left ISRO's mark on the Moon. Its wheels were built to imprint the ISRO logo and the Ashoka emblem into the lunar soil as it rolled.
Your first Indian astronaut crew member may be a robot. ISRO's Gaganyaan test flight will carry Vyommitra, a female-looking humanoid robot that talks and acts as a crew stand-in.
Your cotton seed sprouted on the far side of the Moon. China's Chang'e 4 lander grew a green cotton sprout in 2019, and the photo shows it in a sealed canister.
Your first rock samples from the Moon's far side came home in 2024. China's Chang'e 6 scooped and returned soil from the side that never faces Earth.
Your Earth rises over the Moon's horizon in one famous photo. Apollo 8's Bill Anders took 'Earthrise' in December 1968, and it shows a blue marble above grey ground.
Your phone charger is more powerful than the computer that flew Apollo 11. The Apollo Guidance Computer had about 4 KB of RAM and 72 KB of storage, and the astronauts landed with it.
Your thumbnail held at arm's length covers a patch of sky holding about 10,000 galaxies. Hubble's Ultra Deep Field is a tiny, dark region of the sky, and the image shows galaxy after galaxy.
Your James Webb telescope mirror is 18 gold hexagons. A thin gold coating on each beryllium segment lets it reflect infrared light, and the photos show a giant golden honeycomb.
Your tardigrade survived open space. In 2007, microscopic water bears flew on the Foton-M3 mission, and some came back alive and went on to lay eggs.
Your whole country flies by in minutes from the ISS. At about 7.7 km per second, the station could cross India's roughly 2,900 km east to west width in about 6 minutes, shown on a map.
Your teaspoon of neutron star material would weigh about a billion tonnes. A map animation of the teaspoon next to mountains makes the scale visible.
Your Mercury has ice on it even though daytime hits about 430 degrees C. Ice sits in permanently shadowed craters at the poles, and radar images show the bright patches.
Your sunrise on Mercury can run backwards. At certain spots, the Sun rises, stops, slides back toward the horizon, then rises again, and an animation of the Sun's path shows it.
Your Saturn moon Iapetus is two-toned, one side dark as coal and the other bright as snow. Cassini photos show it, and a huge ridge runs around its equator like a walnut seam.
Your Jupiter moon Io is covered in volcanoes. It is the most volcanically active body in the Solar System, and spacecraft photos show plumes shooting hundreds of km high.
Your Uranus moon Miranda has a cliff about 20 km tall called Verona Rupes. Voyager 2's photo shows a jagged, patchwork moon, and a drop from the cliff would take minutes.
Your Mars canyon, Valles Marineris, would stretch across the United States. It runs about 4,000 km long, and a map overlay on a US map makes the size clear.
Your Mars rover photographed leopard-spot rocks in 2024. Perseverance found 'Cheyava Falls', a rock with spots and streaks that NASA called a possible sign of ancient microbial life.
Your ISS window has a chip in it from a flake of paint. In 2016, a tiny speck about a few thousandths of a mm struck the Cupola, and the photo shows the crack.
Your statue sits on the Moon. Apollo 15 astronauts left 'Fallen Astronaut', a small aluminium figure, near a crater in 1971 to honour those who died in space exploration.
Your message from Earth sits on the Moon on a disc the size of a coin. Apollo 11 left a silicon disc with goodwill messages from 73 countries, shown in the NASA photo.
Your Soyuz capsule fires rockets right before touching down. Rockets blast a cloud of dust just above the Kazakh steppe, softening the landing, and the video shows the burst.
Your first satellite was the size of a beach ball. Sputnik 1, launched in 1957, was 58 cm wide, and its beeps could be heard on radios.
Your dog Laika flew before any human. In November 1957 the Soviet Union sent her into orbit aboard Sputnik 2, and she was the first animal to orbit Earth.
Your Indian-born astronaut flew first in 1997. Kalpana Chawla, born in Karnal, Haryana, became the first Indian-born woman in space aboard Space Shuttle Columbia.
Your Sun is watched from a parking spot a million km away. India's Aditya-L1 reached its Sun-Earth L1 halo orbit in January 2024 and sends back live images of the Sun.
Your Moon is shrinking and wrinkling. NASA's LRO photos show cliffs called lobate scarps on the surface, formed as the Moon's interior slowly cools and contracts.
Your Jupiter has a storm bigger than Earth. The Great Red Spot is about 16,000 km wide, wider than Earth's 12,742 km, and images show Earth placed beside it.
Your teeth, bones and muscles are shown in a spacewalk-style test of astronaut gear. NASA's ISS spacesuit glove check shows a bare hand protected by layers, with the vacuum visible in tests.
